newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian banks gear up for EMU, see FX boost.
newsitem.headline: Asian banks gear up for EMU, see FX boost.

text.p: The launch of a single European currency may be more than two years away, but banks in Asia are already looking at implications for their own business in anticipation the new euro will boost exotic currency trade.
Some banks are already expanding their forex trading teams, while brokers are eyeing the region with hopes for salvation if business dies away in other zones.

But Far Eastern central banks, ever wary of volatility, are likely to take a dim view of anything that begins to resemble the hectic European forex markets of the 1980s and early 1990s, where large speculative flows were commonplace, analysts said.

"With mark/Paris disappearing there's going to be (forex) traders looking for something, anything, to trade. Exotic currency volume is bound to benefit from this," one trader at a U.S. firm here said.
This view was echoed by the head of Treasury at a European bank who said the establishment of the euro was one reason behind an increase in interest in the exotic currency sectors.
"Banks are already beefing up their (exotic currency) desks here. They've brought in some fairly senior people to do this and the euro has to be one of the factors," he said.
He noted that the euro will take away several potential areas of profit for proprietary foreign exchange trading and it was natural that firms involved in the business would look elsewhere.
CURRENCIES MAY BECOME FULLY CONVERTIBLE
"They will look to expand into other currencies. Look for an increase in (Malaysian) ringgit, (Indonesian) rupiah and, to a lesser degree, (Thai) baht trade," he said.
"Basically, all the currencies in this region will ultimately become fully convertible and that's when things could really take off," he predicted.
At present, many currencies in Asia are either tied to the dollar, fixed against a basket of currencies, or -- as in the case of the Singapore dollar -- tightly controlled by a monetary authority.
Desmond Supple, senior emerging markets economist at I.D.E.A. in Singapore, agreed that exotic currency trading volume would get a filip from the creation of the euro.
"The (creation of the) euro will help augment a trend we're already seeing," he said.
He added that he also expected yen cross trading against the exotic currencies to increase. At present virtually all exotic currency trading is conducted through the dollar.
"When it comes to trade and debt flows, the yen is far more important to this region than the dollar," he commented.
The head of Treasury at the European bank concurred.

"For example, over 60 percent of Indonesia's debt is denominated in yen. Indonesia does huge trade with Japan. At present we see some commercial flows in yen/rupiah, but very little in the way of what I call real trading."
"Real trading -- where proprietary traders move in and start having some fun -- will come. I guess it'll happen within three to five years and the euro should hasten the process," he commented.
EFFECT ON FOREIGN EXCHANGE FLOWS UNCERTAIN
I.D.E.A.'s Supple also noted there was still debate as to how the establishment of the euro would affect foreign exchange flows generally -- and by implication the flows in exotic currencies.
"It's extremely contentious whether it (establishment of the euro) will be a positive or a negative for the dollar," he commented.
He said there was a theory that some central banks -- especially those of founder participants in the euro -- would dump some of their dollar holdings to establish a core euro reserve.
But there was also a theory that other central banks around the world would buy dollars to replace their mark reserves. "The fact is, a euro does not equal a mark," he said.
One proprietary exotic currency dealer at a U.S. bank here said that his firm was already looking into expanding its exotic currency trading desk.
"I'm not saying it's all to do with the euro, but the bosses say it's definitely a factor in their thinking," he said.
However, he also commented that until volatility picked up in exotics -- possibly when the euro was established -- profits would not be as great as those offered by trading the mark.

"The central banks try to keep a lid on volatility out here. They're establishing repo pacts between each other to help fend off the speculators. Remember that volatility is what makes traders like me money and at the moment we haven't got too much volatility," he said.
However, he added that a positive sign for the exotic currency market was that brokers were aggressively expanding their presence.
"Electronic broking has taken away a lot of their (brokers) business. The euro will be no different and will almost certainly be largely traded electronically," he said.
He added the euro "would almost certainly be the final nail in the coffin for some brokers unless they look elsewhere -- such as here."
The head of Treasury at the European bank agreed, noting, "Foreign exchange brokers are putting more emphasis on the regionals, the currencies not covered by electronic broking."
But he added a note of caution for banks thinking of expanding here.
"The regionals can be incredibly boring. Perhaps you ought to stick to trading the euro."
